title: Booth Bookings
statement: A recording booth takes reservations measured in whole minutes. A booking [start, end) occupies the minutes start to end - 1, and the booth needs gap cleaning minutes between any two active bookings. Process the operations in order and return one result per operation. ["book", start, end] is accepted only if for every active booking [s, e) either end + gap <= s or e + gap <= start; an accepted booking gets the next id (1, 2, 3, ... counting only accepted bookings) and that id is the result, while a rejected booking changes nothing and the result is -1. ["cancel", id] removes the active booking with that id and returns true, or returns false if the id was never issued or is already cancelled. ["next", time] returns the start minute of the active booking with the smallest start that is at least time, or -1 if there is none. Cancelled ids are never reused.

examples.explanation: Booking [100, 200) gets id 1. [205, 260) starts only 5 minutes after it ends, less than the gap of 10, so it is rejected (-1). [210, 260) starts exactly 10 minutes later and gets id 2. next 150 finds the booking starting at 210. Cancelling id 1 returns true. [150, 205) would end only 5 minutes before [210, 260), so it is rejected, but [150, 200) leaves exactly 10 minutes and gets id 3. Cancelling id 1 again returns false, and next 0 finds the booking starting at 150.

With no gap, back-to-back bookings are fine: [5, 10) is id 1 and [10, 15) is id 2. [9, 11) overlaps both and is rejected. next 6 finds the booking starting at 10. After cancelling id 2 no booking starts at or after minute 6, so next 6 returns -1, and id 7 was never issued.

hints.content: Which already accepted bookings could possibly block a new one? Think about where the new booking would sit if all bookings were in time order.
Active bookings never overlap, so they have a natural order in time. Is every active booking equally able to block a new one, or only some of them?

Keep them sorted by start (their ends are then sorted too), so only the closest booking before and the closest after can be too near. Find the insertion position with a binary search on the starts, then check previous.end + gap <= start and end + gap <= next.start.
Remember each id's start so a cancellation can binary search to its booking and remove it. next is the same binary search: the first start that is at least time.

Binary search is O(log n), but inserting into or removing from a JavaScript array shifts elements, O(n), which is fine for 2,500 bookings. A per-minute calendar costs up to a million steps per operation.

testCases.explanation: A cleaning gap of 10 with a rejected booking on each side of the line.
The largest gap: bookings exactly 1,000 minutes apart are accepted and one placed right after another is rejected.
Bookings at both ends of the day and next at the last minute.
An identical booking is rejected until the first is cancelled, and ids keep counting accepted bookings.
A random mix of 200 operations inside a short day.
A booking near the end of a million-minute day, then alternating next queries and rejected wide bookings: scanning the calendar minute by minute costs hundreds of thousands of steps each.
The largest input of six-digit bookings with the largest gap, which rejects many of them.
The largest mix of books, cancels and next queries over a million-minute day.

solutions.title: A minute-by-minute calendar
solutions.intuition: Mark every booked minute in an array and check the minutes around a new booking directly.
solutions.approach: Keep owner[minute] (the id booked there, 0 if free) and isStart[minute]. A new booking is rejected if any minute from start - gap to end + gap - 1 is owned. Accepting writes the owner for each minute; cancelling clears them; next scans minutes upward from time for the first start mark.
solutions.pseudocode:
book: if any owner[m] != 0 for m in [start-gap, end+gap): reject
      else mark owner[m] = id for m in [start, end); isStart[start] = 1
cancel: clear owner over the booking's minutes; isStart[start] = 0
next: m = time; while m <= 1e6 and not isStart[m]: m += 1
solutions.timeComplexity: O(day length) per operation in the worst case: up to 2,500 * 1,000,000 steps
commonMistakes: Checking only the booking's own minutes and ignoring the cleaning gap on both sides.
Forgetting to clear the start mark on cancel, so next reports a cancelled booking.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A calendar array is the first model most people reach for and it is correct, but every check and every next scans up to a million minutes. Since active bookings never overlap, only their neighbours in time matter, which a sorted list answers with binary search.

steps.title: Book and reject
steps.content: Booking [100, 200) marks minutes 100 to 199. [205, 260) with gap 10 would need minutes 195 to 269 free, but minutes 195 to 199 are owned, so it is rejected.

steps.title: Next
steps.content: next 150 scans minutes 150, 151, ... until the start mark at 210.

solutions.title: Sorted active bookings with binary search
solutions.intuition: Active bookings are disjoint, so sorted by start they are also sorted by end; a new booking can only conflict with its immediate neighbours.
solutions.approach: Keep parallel arrays starts and ends in order, and a map from id to start. For book, binary search the first start >= start, check the predecessor's end + gap <= start and end + gap <= the successor's start, and splice the new booking in. For cancel, look up the start, binary search it and splice it out. For next, return the first start >= time.
solutions.pseudocode:
at = first index with starts[at] >= start
ok = (at == 0 or ends[at-1] + gap <= start) and (at == len or end + gap <= starts[at])
if ok: insert at; ids += 1; startOfId[id] = start
cancel: delete startOfId[id]; remove at the index of that start
next: at = first index with starts[at] >= time
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per search plus O(n) per splice shift, n <= 2,500 active bookings
commonMistakes: Checking every active booking instead of only the two neighbours.
Counting rejected bookings when numbering ids.
Using lower-bound on ends instead of starts, which skips a booking that starts at the same minute.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Non-overlapping intervals form a total order, so a new booking has exactly one predecessor and one successor, and no farther booking can be closer. Binary search finds that position in O(log n). The array splice that keeps the order shifts elements, so the honest worst case is O(n) per accepted booking, which is tiny at 2,500 bookings. A balanced tree would make the update logarithmic too.

steps.title: Insert in order
steps.content: The first booking lands in an empty list; [205, 260) finds predecessor end 200 + 10 = 210 > 205 and is rejected.

steps.title: Place [210, 260)
steps.content: Its predecessor end 200 + 10 = 210 <= 210 passes and there is no successor, so it is inserted as id 2, and next 150 finds starts[1] = 210.
